proof:
# Full-rank sampled projections force coarse volume

This theorem gives a complementary sampling/concentration estimate.
It does not require a dense lattice, a bound on the body, or a common
fiber shape. The resulting OC corollary has an explicit bound on the
number of coarse levels and a displayed small-volume hypothesis.
It is not a proof of unrestricted OC.

## 1. One convex set with a full-rank sampled projection

Let r>=1 and s>=1. Let Q be a compact convex set in R^r_u times
R^s_x. Let L+a be a full-rank lattice coset in R^r, of covolume v.
Let

    P={lambda in L+a: Q_lambda is nonempty},
    T=sum_(lambda in P) vol_s(Q_lambda),
    M=vol_(r+s)(Q).

Assume P is nonempty and affinely spans R^r. Then

    M >= [s!/(r+s)!] v T.                               (1)

Lower-dimensional sampled fibers are allowed; they contribute zero
s-volume but are retained in P and in its affine-rank calculation.
The case T=0 is immediate. For T>0 the same proof shows M>0.

First triangulate conv(P) into r-simplices whose vertices are in P
and in which EVERY point of P is a vertex of some simplex. Such a
triangulation exists: start with any vertex triangulation of the
polytope; insert remaining points one at a time by the stellar
subdivision at the minimal face of the current triangulation that
contains the new point in its relative interior. Subdivide every
incident simplex compatibly along that face. This retains all older
vertices and terminates after finitely many insertions. The resulting
full-dimensional simplices have pairwise disjoint interiors and cover
conv(P). Their volumes are at least v/r!, because their edge
determinants in a lattice basis are nonzero integers.

For one such simplex Delta with vertices lambda_0,...,lambda_r,
put K_i=Q_(lambda_i) and b_i=vol_s(K_i). Its barycentric coordinates
are alpha_i>=0, sum_i alpha_i=1. Convexity gives

    sum_i alpha_i K_i subset Q_(sum_i alpha_i lambda_i).

Brunn--Minkowski and the integer s>=1 imply

    vol_s(Q_(sum alpha_i lambda_i))
       >= (sum_i alpha_i b_i^(1/s))^s
       >= sum_i alpha_i^s b_i.                          (2)

For s=1 the last inequality is equality; for larger integer s it
follows by expanding the nonnegative multinomial terms. Convex sets
of zero s-volume cause no exception in Brunn--Minkowski here.

Integration over an r-simplex gives

    integral_Delta alpha_i^s du
       = vol_r(Delta) r! s!/(r+s)!
       = vol_r(Delta)/binom(r+s,r).                     (3)

For example, slice by alpha_i=t: the remaining simplex has relative
volume (1-t)^(r-1), giving the integral r times
integral_0^1 t^s(1-t)^(r-1)dt; repeated integration by parts gives
the displayed factorial. Thus

    integral_Delta vol_s(Q_u)du
       >= [vol_r(Delta)/binom(r+s,r)] sum_i b_i.

Sum over the triangulation. The simplex volumes are at least v/r!,
and every sampled base occurs in at least one simplex. Positivity of
the b_i therefore yields

    M >= v/[r! binom(r+s,r)] sum_(lambda in P)b_lambda,

which is (1). The body Q may extend beyond conv(P); that only adds
nonnegative volume to the left side. No equality Q=conv(sampled Q)
was used.

The coefficient in (1) is SHARP. Let the sampled projection be a
unimodular r-simplex, put an s-dimensional body K at one vertex,
and put a point at each other vertex. Take their convex hull Q.
The simplex has no other lattice points, so T=vol_s(K). At a base
with barycentric coordinate alpha_0 for the K-vertex, the fiber is
a translate of alpha_0 K. Consequently (3) gives

    M=[v/r!] [r!s!/(r+s)!] vol_s(K)
      =v s!/(r+s)! T.

The hull is full dimensional in R^(r+s). If positive s-volume is
desired at every sampled base, replace the other points by epsilon
homothetic copies of K. As epsilon decreases to zero, the ratio
M/(vT) tends to the same coefficient. Thus this geometric volume
inequality has no hidden constant that can be improved universally.

## 2. Concentration on smaller sampled affine ranks

Let Q_z, z in J, be a finite collection of such compact convex sets
with common lattice L+a, but with no assumption on the ranks of
their sampled projections P_z. Let

    T_z=sum_(lambda in P_z) vol_s((Q_z)_lambda),
    T=sum_z T_z>0,
    M=sum_z vol_(r+s)(Q_z),
    c=(r+s)!/s!.

Let T_full be the sampled mass on levels with affdim P_z=r. Then

    T_full <= c M/v,
    T_def:=T-T_full >= (1-c M/(vT)) T.                  (4)

If the last expression is negative it can be replaced by zero.
This follows by applying (1) only to the full-rank levels and
summing. Levels whose sampled set is empty have T_z=0 and are
irrelevant to the mass; no affine dimension of the empty set is
needed in the definition of T_full.

Thus a sequence with M/(vT)->0 has asymptotically all its sampled
s-volume in levels whose sampled base rank is at most r-1. This is
a statement about the ACTUAL sampled bases. It does not replace
them by an irrational limiting affine plane.

## 3. Exact lower-rank interpretation of a deficient level

Fix one level z with T_z>0 and a sampled projection P_z of affine
rank r'<r. Choose lambda0 in P_z and let V=span(P_z-lambda0).
Since the differences belong to L, the lattice V intersect L has
rank r' and is saturated in L. Choose its integer basis. The affine
plane lambda0+V, with its sampled lattice points, is thereby
identified exactly with R^(r') and Z^(r'), respectively.

Replace Q_z by the hull of ALL its sampled fibers. It has exactly
the same sampled fibers: it is contained in Q_z and contains every
one of those fibers. Its sampled projection is exactly P_z, which
is lattice-convex within lambda0+V. Indeed any lattice base in the
convex hull lies in the original convex projection and so already
belongs to P_z.

This hull is a full convex body in R^(r') times R^s after the base
identification. Its affine span contains the complete s-dimensional
vertical subspace because at least one sampled fiber has positive
s-volume; its base projection spans R^(r'). Thus the full dimension
is r'+s. The change of variables acts only on the base, leaving
each fiber's H_s measure unchanged.

Consequently, if OC is available at integer rank r' and continuous
dimension s, this one level has a point of normalized depth at
least 2^(-r') Gamma_s >=2^(-(r-1)) Gamma_s. Every closed halfspace
of a larger original ambient space restricts to a closed halfspace
on this affine hull, or to its entirety, when it contains the chosen
point. Thus the same bound applies to its contribution inside a
larger mixed set. The r'=0 case is ordinary continuous Grünbaum.

## 4. A conditional sharp-budget corollary for few coarse levels

Suppose the sets Q_z are the actual coarse integer fibers of a
convex body in R^k times R^r times R^s, and let J be the number
of its nonempty SAMPLED coarse levels. Assume

    J<=2^k,
    M/(vT) <= s!/[2(r+s)!].                             (5)

Here M includes the full coarse volumes of ALL nonempty coarse
fibers, including levels with no fine samples; doing so only
strengthens the condition and keeps (4) valid. The sampled total
T is the actual H_s mixed measure before multiplication by v.
Assume OC at integer ranks at most r-1 and continuous dimension s.
Then the original mixed set, with n=k+r integer variables, satisfies
the EXACT target

    max depth >=2^(-k-r) Gamma_s.                       (6)

Indeed (4)--(5) put at least T/2 of the sampled mass on deficient
levels. One of their at most J levels has mass at least T/(2J).
Section 3 supplies a deterministic center in that level. Every
original containing halfspace gets at least its guaranteed mass
from that level alone. Its normalized original depth is at least

    [1/(2J)] 2^(-(r-1)) Gamma_s
       =Gamma_s/(J 2^r) >=2^(-k-r) Gamma_s.

When r=1, only rank zero is invoked; thus this corollary is
unconditional for every s>=1, including arbitrarily large s.
In particular it applies to two adjacent coarse levels (k=1),
and more generally to at most 2^k coarse sampled levels, under
the explicit volume-to-sampled-mass condition (5).

The assumption J<=2^k is not automatic for an arbitrary integer
projection. No claim that (5) always holds is made either. The
rank-deficient mass bound (4) remains valid without those assumptions,
but does not on its own supply a global sharp allocation across
arbitrarily many coarse levels.

## 5. Why s=0 is excluded from this formula

The expansion (2) uses s>=1. For s=0 the analogous sum of alpha_i^0
would overcount the single zero-dimensional fiber. For example an
interval with N+1 sampled endpoints has length Nh and covolume-weighted
count (N+1)h, so (1) with s=0,r=1 would be false. Pure counting OC is
already handled separately by Doignon; no undefined root or 0^0 is
used in this theorem.
